title: Sterilisation — Methods, Validation & Choosing a Process

cards.explanation: An endospore-resistant endpoint distinguishes it from routine disinfection.
cards.text: Sterilisation removes or destroys viable microorganisms including bacterial {{c1::endospores}}.
cards.question: Sterilisation removes or destroys viable microorganisms including bacterial {{c1::endospores}}.

cards.explanation: SAL is a probabilistic process assurance target, not a direct test of every item.
cards.text: A sterility assurance level of 10⁻⁶ means an estimated non-sterile-unit probability of {{c1::one in a million}}.
cards.question: A sterility assurance level of 10⁻⁶ means an estimated non-sterile-unit probability of {{c1::one in a million}}.

cards.explanation: It does not mean the absence of every viable organism under every conceivable condition.
cards.text: Commercial sterility concerns microbes capable of growing under the product's normal {{c1::storage conditions}}.
cards.question: Commercial sterility concerns microbes capable of growing under the product's normal {{c1::storage conditions}}.

cards.explanation: Cleaning, disinfection and validated sterilisation are different objectives.
cards.text: Routine disinfection does not reliably eliminate bacterial {{c1::endospores}}.
cards.question: Routine disinfection does not reliably eliminate bacterial {{c1::endospores}}.

cards.explanation: Pressure permits steam at a higher temperature; pressure alone is not the principal lethal agent.
cards.text: Steam sterilisation acts mainly through moist-heat protein {{c1::denaturation}}.
cards.question: Steam sterilisation acts mainly through moist-heat protein {{c1::denaturation}}.

cards.explanation: The slide pairs this with a typical exposure example. Actual cycle suitability depends on load, steam penetration and validated conditions, not one universal recipe.
cards.text: The example steam-sterilisation temperature in the lecture is {{c1::121°C}}.
cards.question: The example steam-sterilisation temperature in the lecture is {{c1::121°C}}.

cards.explanation: Time and pressure records provide other physical information.
cards.text: An autoclave temperature record is a {{c1::physical}} process check.
cards.question: An autoclave temperature record is a {{c1::physical}} process check.

cards.explanation: A colour change indicates exposure to specified conditions; it does not prove that the entire load is sterile.
cards.text: Autoclave tape is a {{c1::chemical indicator}}.
cards.question: Autoclave tape is a {{c1::chemical indicator}}.

cards.explanation: Biological indicators challenge a validated process with resistant organisms.
cards.text: The spores used as a biological steam-process indicator are {{c1::Geobacillus stearothermophilus}}.
cards.question: The spores used as a biological steam-process indicator are {{c1::Geobacillus stearothermophilus}}.

cards.explanation: It does not establish adequate exposure at every location within the load.
cards.text: A changed tape colour alone cannot establish successful {{c1::sterilisation}}.
cards.question: A changed tape colour alone cannot establish successful {{c1::sterilisation}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture contrasts its higher temperatures and longer exposure with steam.
cards.text: Dry heat damages microbes through oxidation and protein {{c1::denaturation}}.
cards.question: Dry heat damages microbes through oxidation and protein {{c1::denaturation}}.

cards.explanation: The choice depends on moisture compatibility and penetration, not simply whether heat kills microbes.
cards.text: Heat-resistant oils and powders may be suitable for {{c1::dry heat}} rather than steam.
cards.question: Heat-resistant oils and powders may be suitable for {{c1::dry heat}} rather than steam.

cards.explanation: This destroys the material rather than preserving a reusable product.
cards.text: Destruction of contaminated waste by combustion is {{c1::incineration}}.
cards.question: Destruction of contaminated waste by combustion is {{c1::incineration}}.

cards.explanation: It is inappropriate for heat-sensitive plastic devices.
cards.text: Direct flaming is suited to a reusable metal microbiological {{c1::loop}}.
cards.question: Direct flaming is suited to a reusable metal microbiological {{c1::loop}}.

cards.explanation: This permits processing some heat-sensitive liquids.
cards.text: Membrane filtration primarily {{c1::removes}} microorganisms rather than killing them.
cards.question: Membrane filtration primarily {{c1::removes}} microorganisms rather than killing them.

cards.explanation: This is not a universal virus-removal guarantee; retention depends on organism and filter validation.
cards.text: A commonly used bacterial-retention membrane has a nominal pore size of {{c1::0.22 μm}}.
cards.question: A commonly used bacterial-retention membrane has a nominal pore size of {{c1::0.22 μm}}.

cards.explanation: Choose a method compatible with the product and its microbial risks.
cards.text: A heat-sensitive solution may be processed by validated {{c1::membrane filtration}}.
cards.question: A heat-sensitive solution may be processed by validated {{c1::membrane filtration}}.

cards.explanation: It is not by itself proof of complete air sterility or removal of every virus.
cards.text: HEPA filtration removes airborne {{c1::particles}}.
cards.question: HEPA filtration removes airborne {{c1::particles}}.

cards.explanation: The source discusses wavelengths around 253 nm.
cards.text: UV-C prevents replication by damaging microbial {{c1::nucleic acids}}.
cards.question: UV-C prevents replication by damaging microbial {{c1::nucleic acids}}.

cards.explanation: Shadowing and surface geometry can leave organisms inadequately exposed.
cards.text: A major limitation of UV-C is poor {{c1::penetration}}.
cards.question: A major limitation of UV-C is poor {{c1::penetration}}.

cards.explanation: It can sterilise compatible devices within their packaging.
cards.text: Gamma radiation causes lethal DNA damage, including {{c1::strand breaks}}.
cards.question: Gamma radiation causes lethal DNA damage, including {{c1::strand breaks}}.

cards.explanation: This differs from electrically generated electron beams.
cards.text: The gamma source highlighted in the lecture is {{c1::cobalt-60}}.
cards.question: The gamma source highlighted in the lecture is {{c1::cobalt-60}}.

cards.explanation: It causes DNA damage with a relatively low thermal impact.
cards.text: Electron-beam processing uses high-energy {{c1::electrons}}.
cards.question: Electron-beam processing uses high-energy {{c1::electrons}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture also highlights higher energy requirements; exact ratios depend on equipment.
cards.text: Compared with electron beams, X-rays provide greater {{c1::penetration}} into suitable loads.
cards.question: Compared with electron beams, X-rays provide greater {{c1::penetration}} into suitable loads.

cards.explanation: It offers low-temperature processing of compatible heat-sensitive devices.
cards.text: Ethylene oxide kills by {{c1::alkylating}} proteins and nucleic acids.
cards.question: Ethylene oxide kills by {{c1::alkylating}} proteins and nucleic acids.

cards.explanation: Ethylene oxide is the lecture example; compatibility, residues and validated aeration matter.
cards.text: A heat-sensitive electronic device may require low-temperature {{c1::gas sterilisation}}.
cards.question: A heat-sensitive electronic device may require low-temperature {{c1::gas sterilisation}}.

cards.explanation: The source includes room decontamination and compatible medical devices.
cards.text: Vapourised hydrogen peroxide acts through {{c1::oxidative damage}}.
cards.question: Vapourised hydrogen peroxide acts through {{c1::oxidative damage}}.

cards.explanation: They provide a low-temperature option for compatible delicate instruments.
cards.text: Hydrogen peroxide gas-plasma systems generate damaging {{c1::free radicals}}.
cards.question: Hydrogen peroxide gas-plasma systems generate damaging {{c1::free radicals}}.

cards.explanation: Exposure toxicity is a major limitation; the slide's future regulatory prediction is not treated as established law.
cards.text: Formaldehyde can kill by cross-linking proteins and {{c1::nucleic acids}}.
cards.question: Formaldehyde can kill by cross-linking proteins and {{c1::nucleic acids}}.

cards.explanation: A validated process and device compatibility remain necessary.
cards.text: The liquid oxidising sterilant highlighted for compatible flexible endoscopes is {{c1::peracetic acid}}.
cards.question: The liquid oxidising sterilant highlighted for compatible flexible endoscopes is {{c1::peracetic acid}}.

cards.explanation: The mechanism is damage to cellular components.
cards.text: Ozone acts as an {{c1::oxidising}} gaseous sterilant.
cards.question: Ozone acts as an {{c1::oxidising}} gaseous sterilant.

cards.explanation: It combines high temperature with short exposure in suitable food-processing systems.
cards.text: UHT stands for {{c1::ultra-high temperature}} processing.
cards.question: UHT stands for {{c1::ultra-high temperature}} processing.

cards.explanation: Its shelf stability also depends on the packaging and storage conditions.
cards.text: Shelf-stable UHT milk is an example of {{c1::commercial sterility}}.
cards.question: Shelf-stable UHT milk is an example of {{c1::commercial sterility}}.

cards.explanation: The aim is commercial sterility and shelf stability rather than a universal medical-device endpoint.
cards.text: A retort processes packaged foods using a specialised {{c1::heat treatment}}.
cards.question: A retort processes packaged foods using a specialised {{c1::heat treatment}}.

cards.explanation: Heat, pressure, chemicals and radiation have distinct occupational hazards.
cards.text: A sterilisation process must protect the operator as well as the {{c1::product}}.
cards.question: A sterilisation process must protect the operator as well as the {{c1::product}}.

cards.explanation: No one technique suits every product.
cards.text: The appropriate sterilisation method depends on material compatibility and the required {{c1::sterility assurance}}.
cards.question: The appropriate sterilisation method depends on material compatibility and the required {{c1::sterility assurance}}.

cards.explanation: Successful processing depends on conditions throughout the relevant load.
cards.text: A process must be {{c1::validated}} rather than assumed effective from the machine name.
cards.question: A process must be {{c1::validated}} rather than assumed effective from the machine name.

slides.topic: Sterilisation — Methods, Validation & Choosing a Process — source 2
slides.text:
Learning objectives
Recall the definition of microbial ‘sterilisation’, and describe what it does and does not represent

Describe the processes of methods of sterilisation

Critically evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of sterilisation techniques, andtheir appropriateness for specific products/situations

slides.topic: Sterilisation — Methods, Validation & Choosing a Process — source 3
slides.text:
Starter Activity
What do all these products have in common?

slides.topic: Sterilisation — Methods, Validation & Choosing a Process — source 4
slides.text:
What is the healthcare/scientific definition of ‘sterile’?
The standard definition used in healthcare and microbiology is: “free from any viable microorganisms or endospores”

For medical devices (catheters, syringes, etc.), manufacturers must meet a Sterility Assurance Level (SAL) of 10-6

This means there is no more than a 1 in 1,000,000 probability of a viableorganism being on a piece of sterilised equipment

slides.topic: Sterilisation — Methods, Validation & Choosing a Process — source 5
slides.text:
What is the food industry definition of ‘sterile’?
In food microbiology, the term ‘commercial sterility’ is commonly used

In this case, ‘sterile’ does not mean‘free from all viable microorganismsor endospores’ 

It means that: ‘microorganisms capableof growing under the normal storage conditions of the product have been eliminated’

slides.topic: Sterilisation — Methods, Validation & Choosing a Process — source 6
slides.text:
Comparing sterilisation and disinfection
Feature | Sterilisation | Disinfection
Eliminates bacteria | ✅ | Not necessarily entirely
Eliminates fungi | ✅ | Not necessarily entirely
Eliminates viruses | ✅ | Not necessarily entirely
Eliminates bacterial endospores | ✅ | ❌
Absolute endpoint? | ✅ | ❌
Examples of methods | Steam sterilisation (autoclave), dry heat sterilisation, incineration, direct flaming, filtration (membrane), gamma irradiation, electron beam irradiation, X-ray sterilisation, UV light (in some cases), Ethylene oxide (EtO), Hydrogen peroxide vapour (VHP), Hydrogen peroxide gas, formaldehyde gas, peracetic acid, ozone, retort sterilisation, ultra-heat treated (UHT), High-Efficiency Particulate Air Filter (HEPA) | Alcohol, bleach, quaternary ammonium compounds
Example outcome | Sterile catheter | Disinfected work surface

slides.topic: Sterilisation — Methods, Validation & Choosing a Process — source 7
slides.text:
Moist heat steam sterilisation (autoclaving)
Denatures and coagulates proteins / nucleic acids

High temperature (121°C)

Short length of time  (15 minutes)

High pressure (15 psi)

Eliminates all viruses,bacteria, fungi, protists,helminths, & endospores

slides.topic: Sterilisation — Methods, Validation & Choosing a Process — source 8
slides.text:
Checking heat sterilisation conditions havebeen reached
Physical methods of checking:
- Thermocouples data loggers (show temperature)- Pressure gauges and transducers (show pressure)- Autoclave printouts (time, temp., pressure history)

Chemical methods of checking:
- Autoclave tape shows conditions were reached- Browne’s tubes show conditions were reached(Red  Green colour change)

Biological methods of checking:- Use Geobacillus stearothermophilus sporesas a control to see if autoclaving is working correctly

slides.topic: Sterilisation — Methods, Validation & Choosing a Process — source 9
slides.text:
Dry heat sterilisation
Works via causing oxidative damage and protein denaturation

160-180°C for 2 to 3 hours(!)

Used extensively on glassware, metal instruments, powders, oils

Think critically – why not usesteam on those products instead?

slides.topic: Sterilisation — Methods, Validation & Choosing a Process — source 10
slides.text:
Incineration sterilisation
Extremely high temperature (>800°C)

Complete combustion ofmicroorganisms and materials

Used to destroy disposable loops, L-shaped spreaders, plastics, and any clinical waste

slides.topic: Sterilisation — Methods, Validation & Choosing a Process — source 11
slides.text:
Direct flaming sterilisation
Use of a Bunsen burner flamewith a nichrome microbiologicalloop (which reaches 700°C-1000°C)

Rapid oxidation and burning of thematerial on the loop

Used extensively in academic,clinical, and commercial settings

slides.topic: Sterilisation — Methods, Validation & Choosing a Process — source 12
slides.text:
Filtration (membrane sterilisation)
Typically using a 0.22μm filter(20 nm used to filter out viruses!)

Physically removes microorganismsfrom a sample

Primarily used in antibiotic solutions, vaccines, serum, and heat-sensitive media

slides.topic: Sterilisation — Methods, Validation & Choosing a Process — source 13
slides.text:
High-Efficiency Particulate Air Filter (HEPA)sterilisation 
≥99.97% removal of 0.3μm particles

Physically removes airborne microorganisms…must be used alongside another step for true ‘sterility’ and to clear viruses

Used in clean rooms, biological safety cabinets

slides.topic: Sterilisation — Methods, Validation & Choosing a Process — source 14
slides.text:
Ultraviolet (UV) irradiation sterilisation
UV-C radiation (around 253nm wavelength) damage nucleic acidsand prevent microbial replication

Effective against bacteria, fungi, viruses,and bacterial spores (at higher ‘doses’)
Very poor penetrative power… only works where the light directly reaches
Still used on flat surfaces and whereshadows can be controlled

slides.topic: Sterilisation — Methods, Validation & Choosing a Process — source 15
slides.text:
Gamma irradiation sterilisation
Sterilises by causing DNA strand breaks via ionising gamma ray radiation

Usually uses the radioactive Cobalt-60 isotope as the source of the radiation

Commonly used to sterilise syringes, catheters, gloves, Pasteur pipettes, L-shaped spreaders, most single-use plastics, that are already in their packages

Can use Bacillus pumilus as a controlto check sterilisation occurs correctly

slides.topic: Sterilisation — Methods, Validation & Choosing a Process — source 16
slides.text:
Electron beam irradiation sterilisation
High-energy electrons are used to cause fatal DNA damage inmicroorganisms 

Used to sweep a curtain ofhigh-energy electrons atpackaged medical devices

No radioactive waste generated,completes in minutes, verylow thermal impact

slides.topic: Sterilisation — Methods, Validation & Choosing a Process — source 17
slides.text:
X-ray sterilisation
High-energy X-rays cause extensive,fatal DNA damage in microorganisms

Used in the generation of sterilemedical devices and pharmaceuticals

X-rays are disorganised and can scatterwidely

Provides excellent penetration into surfaces

X-ray systems use 10 times as much energy compared to electron beam systems(!)

slides.topic: Sterilisation — Methods, Validation & Choosing a Process — source 18
slides.text: Electron Beam versus X-Ray Sterilisation

slides.topic: Sterilisation — Methods, Validation & Choosing a Process — source 19
slides.text:
Ethylene oxide (EtO) gas sterilisation
Low-temperature gaseous process which exploits the alkylation of DNA and proteins to destroy microorganisms 

Used to sterile catheters, endoscopes, electronics, and plastics

Modern hospitals have thesemachines in-house

Bacillus subtilis can be used as a controlto check sterilisation occurs correctly

slides.topic: Sterilisation — Methods, Validation & Choosing a Process — source 20
slides.text:
Hydrogen peroxide vapour (VHP) sterilisation
Uses vapourised hydrogen peroxide tocause oxidative damage to microbecellular components

Used to decontaminate an entire room/ward after an outbreak,and sterilise medical devices

Used by the NHS to destroy Clostridioides difficile spores, norovirus, MRSA, and other persistent pathogens

slides.topic: Sterilisation — Methods, Validation & Choosing a Process — source 21
slides.text:
Hydrogen peroxide gas plasma sterilisation
Low-temperature plasma processcauses free-radical mediateddamage to microorganisms 

Used to treat delicate, heat-sensitive or moisture sensitive surgicalinstruments (endoscopes, etc.)

Used extensively by the NHS for thispurpose

slides.topic: Sterilisation — Methods, Validation & Choosing a Process — source 22
slides.text:
Formaldehyde gas fumigation sterilisation
A low-temperature gaseous process

Formaldehyde acts as a very strong alkylating agent, causing cross-links to form between DNA, proteins, nucleic acids

Historical extensive use in ‘formaldehyde bombs’ to sterilise hospital wards

Extremely controversial at the moment,NHS staff may have been exposedabove long-term safety limits… new regulations pending 2027

slides.topic: Sterilisation — Methods, Validation & Choosing a Process — source 23
slides.text: Think of the reasons that this method is beingphased out…

slides.topic: Sterilisation — Methods, Validation & Choosing a Process — source 24
slides.text:
Peracetic acid sterilisation
Peracetic acid is a liquid chemicalsterilant

Causes extensive oxidation of proteins and membranes of microorganisms

Used to sterilise flexible endoscopes (like those used in colonoscopies), and otherheat-sensitive equipment

slides.topic: Sterilisation — Methods, Validation & Choosing a Process — source 25
slides.text:
Ozone sterilisation
Oxidative gaseous sterilant

Causes the oxidation of cellular components of the microbes

Also used as a specialistmethod for the sterilisationof medical devices

slides.topic: Sterilisation — Methods, Validation & Choosing a Process — source 26
slides.text:
Ultra-High Temperature (UHT) sterilisation
135-150°C for 2 to 5 seconds(!)

Causes the thermal destruction ofmicroorganisms, leading to the commercial definition of ‘sterility’

Used on shelf-stable milk, beverages, and ready-to-consume infant milk

slides.topic: Sterilisation — Methods, Validation & Choosing a Process — source 27
slides.text:
Food retort sterilisation
Essentially a ‘specialised’ autoclave…

Designed to process packaged foods(canned soup, cans of veg., ready meals)

Achieve ‘commercial sterility’ – meaning that no microorganisms that are capable of growing under the intended storage conditions can survive

Concerned with food safety and shelfstability rather than absolute sterility as we define it clinically

slides.topic: Sterilisation — Methods, Validation & Choosing a Process — source 28
slides.text:
Please keep yourself safe if you workwith sterilisation techniques in the future!
Ensure that your employer and yourself are compliant with:
Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974
Control of Substances Hazardous to Health Regulations (COSHH)
Pressure Systems Safety Regulations 2000 (PSSR)
HSE Safety Requirements for Autoclaves (PM73)
NHS England Health Technical Memorandum (HTM) 01-01
Ionising Radiations Regulations 2017 (IRR17)
Local Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs); Risk Assessments; COSHH Assessments

The same technologies that kill microorganisms can also very easily kill you too!

slides.topic: Sterilisation — Methods, Validation & Choosing a Process — source 30
slides.text:
Summary
True sterilisation is: ‘the complete destruction or removal of viable microorganisms, including highly resistant forms such as bacterial endospores’. This differs to ‘disinfection’

Different materials require different sterilisation methods; no single technique is suitable for all products or applications

Successful sterilisation depends on validated processesthat achieve the required level of sterility assurancewhile maintaining the product’s safety and functionality
